Oracle database found
 Potential 8
FilePosition
pom.xmlLine 52
docker-compose.ymlLine 32
src/main/resources/application-docker.propertiesLine 3
src/main/resources/application.propertiesLine 12
src/main/resources/application-docker.propertiesLine 6
src/main/resources/application.propertiesLine 15

Explanation

Oracle database found. To migrate a Java application that uses an Oracle database to Azure, you can follow these recommendations:

* Migrate to Azure Database for PostgreSQL: Azure recommends migrating Oracle databases to Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server as it provides better cost-effectiveness and performance. Create a managed PostgreSQL Flexible Server database in Azure and choose the appropriate pricing tier based on your application's requirements.

* Use migration tools: Utilize the Azure Database Migration Service (DMS) or third-party tools to migrate your Oracle database schema and data to PostgreSQL. Consider using ora2pg or similar tools to convert Oracle-specific SQL to PostgreSQL-compatible SQL.

* Update database drivers and connection strings: Replace Oracle JDBC drivers with PostgreSQL drivers in your Java application. Update connection strings from Oracle format (jdbc:oracle:thin:) to PostgreSQL format (jdbc:postgresql:).

* Review and convert Oracle-specific code: Identify and convert Oracle-specific SQL functions, stored procedures, and PL/SQL code to PostgreSQL equivalents. Pay attention to data types, syntax differences, and built-in functions.

* Enable monitoring and diagnostics: Utilize Azure Monitor to gain insights into the performance and health of your Java application and the underlying PostgreSQL database. Set up metrics, alerts, and log analytics to proactively identify and resolve issues.

* Implement security measures: Apply security best practices to protect your Java application and the PostgreSQL database. This includes implementing authentication and authorization mechanisms with passwordless connections and leveraging Microsoft Defender for Cloud for threat detection and vulnerability assessments.

* Backup your data: Azure Database for PostgreSQL provides automated backups by default. You can configure the retention period for backups based on your requirements. You can also enable geo-redundant backups, if needed, to enhance data durability and availability.
Password found in configuration file
 Potential 3
FilePosition
src/test/resources/application-test.propertiesLine 5
src/test/resources/application-test.propertiesLine 23
src/main/resources/application-docker.propertiesLine 5
src/main/resources/application.propertiesLine 14

Explanation

Using clear passwords in property files is a security risk, as they can be easily compromised if the files are accessed by unauthorized individuals. To enhance the security of your application, it is recommended to employ secure credential management practices.

* Azure Key Vault: Utilize Azure Key Vault to securely store and manage your application's passwords and other sensitive credentials. Azure Key Vault provides a centralized and highly secure location for storing secrets, keys, and certificates.

* Passwordless connections: You can provide an additional layer of security and convenience for accessing resources in Azure by eliminating the need for passwords. This way you can reduce the risk of password-related vulnerabilities, such as weak passwords or password theft.

The application is setting the server port. To migrate a Java application that sets the server port to Azure Container Apps:

Restricted configurations found
 Potential 2
FilePosition
src/main/resources/application-docker.propertiesLine 25
src/main/resources/application.propertiesLine 2

Explanation

The application uses restricted configurations for Azure Container Apps.
These properties can be automatically injected into your application environment by Azure Container Apps to access managed Config Server and managed Eureka Server.
Please remove them from your application, including configuration files, config server files, command line parameters, Java system attributes, and environment variables.

If configured in configuration files: they will be ignored and overrided by Azure Container Apps.

If configured in Config Server files, command line parameters, Java system attribute, environment variable: they need to be removed or you might experience conflicts and unexpected behavior.

Detects usage of Jakarta Persistence (JPA) APIs
 Potential 5
FilePosition
pom.xmlLine 46

Explanation

The application depends on Jakarta Persistence (JPA) APIs (jakarta.persistence. or legacy javax.persistence.), which are used for object-relational mapping (ORM) and database interaction in Jakarta EE or Java EE applications.

When migrating to Azure:

  • Ensure that the database connection, JPA provider (e.g., Hibernate, EclipseLink), and dialect are compatible with your target Azure database service.
  • Recommended database services include Azure Database for PostgreSQL, Azure Database for MySQL, or Azure SQL Database.
  • For containerized deployments, these JPA-based applications can run on Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) or Azure App Service for Linux/Windows.
  • If using Spring Data JPA, verify that connection pool settings and environment variables are properly configured for the cloud environment.
  • Consider leveraging Azure Key Vault for secure storage of database credentials and connection strings.

Explanation

The application is using a Spring Boot version that has reached its End of OSS Support.
With the officially supported new versions from Spring, you can get the best experience. Here are some steps you can take to update your application to the latest version of Spring Boot:

  • Choose a supported Spring Boot version: Check out Spring Boot Support Versions and determine the most suitable supported Spring Boot version.
  • Update Spring Boot version: Update the Spring Boot version of your application. There are automated tools like Rewrite to help you with the migration.
  • Address code compatibility: Review your application's codebase for any potential compatibility issues with the target Spring Boot version. Update deprecated APIs or features, address any language or library changes, and ensure that your code follows best practices and standards.
  • Test thoroughly: Execute a comprehensive testing process to verify the compatibility and functionality of your application with the new Spring Boot version. Perform unit tests, integration tests, and system tests to validate that all components and dependencies work as expected.

Upgrading to a supported version ensures better performance, security, and compatibility with modern tools.

4. Thoroughly Test: Run unit, integration, and end-to-end tests to make sure everything still works after the upgrade.

Data Storage & External Services

Oracle stores photo metadata and image bytes in the photos table; the photo_data field is a JPA LOB. Uploaded bytes are written to the database, and /photo/{id} returns those bytes through a ByteArrayResource; /uploads/ paths are compatibility metadata, not the current upload storage mechanism (entity, upload persistence, image response). Compose persists Oracle files in oracle_data and mounts oracle-init for database initialization (volume mounts). Both application profiles set spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=create, so schema recreation on startup is configured despite the persistent database volume (default configuration, Docker profile).

The browser fetches Bootstrap assets from jsDelivr; no application-side cache, message broker, object-storage integration, or external business API was identified in the inspected build, configuration and source. Database and administrator credentials are supplied through external configuration/environment variables; no values are reproduced here (Compose wiring, administrator configuration).

Key Architectural Decisions

  • Layered monolith with constructor injection: MVC controllers depend on the PhotoService interface; its implementation injects PhotoRepository. Read methods use read-only transactions within a transactional service (controller injection, service injection and transactions).
  • Database-centric photo storage: JPA entities carry metadata and BLOB content together; native queries use Oracle constructs such as ROWNUM, NVL, and TO_CHAR, coupling persistence to Oracle (mapping, queries).
  • Public gallery with protected mutations: an in-memory administrator is configured with BCrypt; HTTP Basic authenticates upload/delete requests, sessions are stateless and CSRF is explicitly disabled. No TLS termination is configured in the inspected application/Compose settings (security policy, HTTP port, published port).

API & Service Communication Contracts

Five explicit application endpoints provide gallery/detail HTML, multipart upload with JSON results, binary photo retrieval, and deletion by POST. Requests use synchronous controller-to-service calls; no application messaging or downstream HTTP API client was identified.

Upload contract details:

  • Normal batch responses contain success, uploadedPhotos, and failedUploads. success means at least one uploaded photo was added to the response, not that every file succeeded. Failed items contain fileName and error; the empty-list 400 response instead contains success: false and error. HomeController.java:58–97
  • Successful entries are manually selected metadata projections, not serialized Photo entities or binary payloads. A successful upload is followed by a lookup; if that lookup returns empty, the controller adds neither a success entry nor a failure entry for that item. HomeController.java:68–90
  • Per-file rejection and caught upload-processing failures become failed entries in a 200 batch result. No controller advice standardizes multipart-limit or uncaught transaction/lookup failures into this JSON envelope. Individual validation rules belong in business-workflows.md; multipart limit configuration belongs in configuration-inventory.md. PhotoServiceImpl.java:82–193

Binary responses set Cache-Control: no-cache, no-store, must-revalidate, private, Pragma: no-cache, Expires: 0, and X-Photo-ID, X-Photo-Name, X-Photo-Size. The upload metadata's compatibility filePath is not the implemented binary retrieval contract; clients construct /photo/{id}. PhotoFileController.java:74–83, PhotoServiceImpl.java:112–115, upload.js:178–179

Framework-served CSS, JavaScript, and packaged static resources are not additional controller business endpoints. There is no explicit GET-list JSON API, HTTP DELETE route, or endpoint exposing the repository's additional query methods. Controller mappings above; repository methods

Communication Patterns

  • Browser-to-application: Same-origin HTTP requests; upload JavaScript creates FormData, awaits fetch('/upload'), parses JSON only on successful HTTP status, and displays a generic error otherwise. JavaScript promises do not indicate backend queue/event processing. upload.js:90–132
  • Internal synchronous calls: Controllers inject PhotoService; PhotoServiceImpl calls PhotoRepository synchronously, with transactions around service operations. The repository uses JPA/JDBC to the database through the Compose hostname oracle-db, not service-registry discovery. Service calls and transactions, repository, connection wiring
  • Composition: Upload combines per-file service results into one batch envelope, and detail rendering combines a photo with previous/next navigation IDs. Both are in-process composition, not gateway fan-out to independent services. No API gateway, registry client/server, client-side load balancer, gRPC client, message broker, pub/sub, or event-driven application integration was identified. Upload aggregation, detail composition, dependencies
  • Resilience and timeouts: No application retry, circuit breaker, bulkhead, fallback service, explicit HTTP-client timeout, or transaction/query timeout was found. Consequently no application timeout value can be reported; library defaults are not treated as explicit policies. Error behavior is local: gallery becomes empty, detail redirects, deletion redirects with a failure flash message, binary serving returns 404/500, and uploads collect per-file errors. The browser does not implement retries or an explicit fetch timeout. Compose process restart is not request-level retry. Controller sources above; service error handling, browser handling, restart declaration
  • Startup/API availability: Compose starts the app only after database health is satisfied; database connectivity and provision of the required administrator password are prerequisites for normal application startup. Detailed startup/configuration information belongs in configuration-inventory.md. Dependency, administrator creation
  • Authentication and authorization: Stateless HTTP Basic is enabled. POST /upload and /detail/*/delete require authentication; other requests are permitted by the filter chain. An in-memory account is assigned an ADMIN role, but the routes require only authentication, not an ADMIN role check. CSRF is explicitly disabled. No JWT/OAuth2 flow or method-level authorization is implemented in the inspected source. Credentials are intentionally not reproduced. SecurityConfig.java:33–61
  • Transport security: No application HTTPS listener, TLS termination service, HTTPS requirement, or encrypted JDBC configuration is shown in the inspected application/Compose configuration. Do not assume HTTP Basic credentials are protected in transit without an externally configured TLS terminator. Bootstrap assets are loaded separately by the browser over HTTPS from jsDelivr; this is a frontend asset dependency, not backend service communication. Application listener/configuration, Compose topology, template asset reference
  • Browser authentication integration: Upload JavaScript sets no explicit Authorization header or login flow; protected actions therefore rely on an already authenticated browser HTTP Basic context or a caller providing credentials. A fresh unauthenticated upload receives the security-layer failure rather than a batch upload result. upload.js:102–127, Basic authentication policy

Startup Dependency Chain

  1. Compose interpolation → required environment inputs: Oracle and application administrator secrets must be supplied before containers can be created (docker-compose.yml:6-9,30-36). Values remain [REDACTED].
  2. Oracle container → initialization scripts: Compose mounts oracle-init into the image initialization directory and persists database files. The shell initializer checks required variables and waits a fixed 30 seconds before its SQL work (docker-compose.yml:12-14; oracle-init/create-user.sh:9-22). The image also receives application-user environment variables (docker-compose.yml:8-9).
  3. Application container → waits for Oracle healthy: depends_on uses condition: service_healthy. Oracle runs the image-provided healthcheck.sh every 30 seconds, with a 10-second timeout, 15 retries, and 180-second start period (docker-compose.yml:17-22,39-41). These are health-check parameters, not a single declared overall startup timeout.
  4. Spring context → datasource and required administrator property: Base/Docker datasource password placeholder and code-injected administrator password have no fallback (src/main/resources/application.properties:14; src/main/resources/application-docker.properties:5; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/config/SecurityConfig.java:34-37). No config-server/discovery-server stage, application health check, custom startup retry, or wait-for-TCP wrapper is defined.
  5. Azure script, separate provisioning chain: Existing Azure CLI login → resource group → ACR → AKS → ACR attachment → PostgreSQL → database/firewall configuration → 30-second fixed wait → SQL initialization → .env output (azure-setup.ps1:43-58,69-127,139-197,207-299). No application deployment/readiness stage is established by these provisioning operations.

oracle-init/healthcheck.sql:1-3 is a standalone SQL check; Compose invokes healthcheck.sh, not this SQL file directly. SQL grant/verification files contain fixed schema identifiers while the shell initializer accepts APP_USER; changing that credential input does not automatically parameterize all SQL scripts (oracle-init/01-create-user.sql:15-30; oracle-init/02-verify-user.sql:5-12).

Secrets Provisioning Workflow

  • Local containers: Operator copies .env.example to ignored .env, supplies secrets, then Compose interpolates them into Oracle and application environments (.env.example:1-17; .gitignore:201-204; Compose:6-9,30-36). Oracle receives its administrative password and application credentials; Spring receives datasource and administrator credentials. The initializer uses environment inputs for SQL authentication/user creation (oracle-init/create-user.sh:11-35). No external secret-store retrieval or encrypted-property layer is configured.
  • Application identity: Spring creates an in-memory administrator from injected properties and encodes the supplied password with the configured password encoder (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/config/SecurityConfig.java:28-42). Database access uses username/password credentials; no application managed-identity binding is shown.
  • Azure provisioning: The script requires an existing Azure CLI session, accepts or generates database passwords with a cryptographic random-number generator, provisions resources/users, and writes application connection material to ignored .env (azure-setup.ps1:15-22,35-48,117-127,207-299). AKS is attached to ACR for image-pull access (azure-setup.ps1:99-105); ACR administrative access is enabled (azure-setup.ps1:69-74). No application identity assignment, Key Vault permission grant, Kubernetes Secret binding, or PostgreSQL-to-Spring secret binding is present.
  • Storage/encryption limits: .env is written as plaintext with Out-File; ignore rules prevent normal tracking but are not encryption or a file-permission policy (azure-setup.ps1:283-299; .gitignore:201-204). No Jasypt, sealed secrets, or equivalent application secret encryption configuration was found. All actual values are intentionally omitted here.

Core Business Workflows

Photo Album lets visitors browse a shared photo gallery and inspect individual pictures with chronological navigation. Authenticated users can add pictures in batches and permanently remove pictures from the gallery.

Domain Entities

EntityService / Bounded ContextDescriptionKey Relationships
PhotoPhotoService / Photo managementAn uploaded picture, including its display information and image content; the only persisted business entity identified.Each photo stands alone in the shared gallery. Older/newer neighbors are derived from upload time, not explicit relationships. No album, user ownership, or tagging entity is modeled.
UploadResultPhotoService / Upload processingA transient operation outcome, not a persisted entity or aggregate. Communicates acceptance or rejection of one uploaded file.A successful result references the saved Photo; a failed result carries the submitted filename and an error.

Evidence: Photo.java:12–108, UploadResult.java:3–29, PhotoServiceImpl.java:220–237.

Service-to-Domain Mapping

This is one application with internal layers, not independently deployed business services. The following rows describe responsibilities within that application.

ServiceDomain ContextOwned EntitiesExternal Dependencies
HomeController and browser upload UIShared gallery and batch-upload presentationNo independent entity ownership; composes Photo summaries and UploadResult outcomesPhotoService; visitor's browser
DetailControllerIndividual-photo viewing and removalNo independent entity ownership; reads/deletes Photo through PhotoServicePhotoService
PhotoFileControllerDelivery of picture contentNo independent entity ownership; reads Photo contentPhotoService
PhotoServiceImpl with PhotoRepositoryPhoto management, authoritative business operations and persistencePhoto; transient UploadResultPhoto database; image-header readers
SecurityConfigWrite-access controlNo business entity; configured authentication accountExternally supplied credentials, omitted from this document

PhotoService owns the business operations; the repository-backed photo database is the source of truth for both metadata and image bytes. Controllers do not maintain separate stores or exchange events. Evidence: HomeController.java:24–97, DetailController.java:18–78, PhotoFileController.java:23–83, PhotoServiceImpl.java:28–47, SecurityConfig.java:33–60.

Primary Workflows

Workflow 1: Upload pictures and refresh the gallery

  1. A user selects or drops files. The browser applies Client upload screening, reports rejected selections, and sends accepted files to POST /upload.
  2. The security filter requires Authenticated writes before the controller runs. The controller applies Nonempty batch and processes each supplied file sequentially.
  3. PhotoService applies Server upload acceptance and Image-dimension safety. It reads the content, extracts dimensions when supported, and generates a compatibility filename/path.
  4. The service constructs a Photo, assigning its identity and upload time, and saves metadata and image bytes together through PhotoRepository. No separate filesystem upload is performed.
  5. For each successful UploadResult, HomeController reloads the Photo and builds a display summary. Failed outcomes are collected separately; one rejection does not deliberately stop subsequent files.
  6. The controller returns accepted summaries and per-file failures. The browser prepends cards for accepted photos and displays returned errors without a page reload. Cards subsequently retrieve image content separately.

There is no batch-wide all-or-nothing transaction. Normal processing can produce mixed success. A success whose follow-up lookup returns no photo is omitted from both result lists; a follow-up lookup exception is not caught by the controller and can interrupt the response after earlier saves.

Evidence: upload.js:48–132, upload.js:135–179, HomeController.java:55–97, PhotoServiceImpl.java:81–192, Photo.java:93–107.

Workflow 2: Browse the gallery and inspect adjacent pictures

  1. A visitor opens GET /. HomeController requests all photos, ordered newest first, and renders the shared gallery. If retrieval throws, it logs the failure and renders an empty list rather than an explicit unavailable-gallery response.
  2. Selecting a picture enters GET /detail/{id}. The controller looks up the current Photo and requests older/newer neighbors under Chronological navigation.
  3. The detail page combines the current photo with optional previous/next identifiers. A missing or blank identifier, missing photo, or detail-loading exception redirects to the gallery.
  4. Gallery/detail image elements independently request GET /photo/{id}. PhotoFileController reads stored bytes and serves them using the recorded MIME type. Missing records or empty image data return not found; other serving exceptions return a server error.

Evidence: HomeController.java:37–49, DetailController.java:32–58, PhotoServiceImpl.java:53–75, PhotoServiceImpl.java:223–237, detail.html:67–87, PhotoFileController.java:37–86.

Workflow 3: Confirm and permanently remove a picture

  1. The detail-page delete form requests browser confirmation before submitting POST /detail/{id}/delete. This confirmation is a UI affordance, not a server-side approval step.
  2. The security filter applies Authenticated writes. PhotoService looks up the Photo; absence returns false, while presence causes repository deletion of the record and its stored image content.
  3. DetailController sets a success message, a not-found message, or a retry-oriented error message following an exception, then redirects to the gallery. No soft-delete, restore, or compensating business operation is implemented.

Evidence: detail.html:50–51, DetailController.java:64–78, PhotoServiceImpl.java:198–217, SecurityConfig.java:45–60.

The application entry point only starts the application. No scheduled jobs, message listeners, batch commands, or startup business-state initialization were identified in the application source. Repository methods for monthly filtering, pagination, and statistics are not connected to the traced controller workflows and are not documented as user-facing processes. Evidence: PhotoAlbumApplication.java:9–14, PhotoRepository.java:58–100.

Cross-Service Data Flows

  • No remote business-service aggregation: controllers call one in-process PhotoService, which reads/writes the same authoritative photo store. There is no gateway, message choreography, circuit breaker, or cross-context identifier reconciliation in the traced code.
  • Batch result composition: the upload service returns one outcome per processed file; the controller joins successful outcomes back to Photo by returned photo ID, then composes accepted summaries and failure messages. Image bytes are not included in that response.
  • Detail composition: the controller combines a current Photo with neighbors selected by upload time. The browser loads the image by the same photo ID, rather than using the compatibility upload path.
  • Degradation: gallery lookup failures appear as an empty gallery; detail failures redirect home; absent image data returns not found. Upload failures normally remain per-file outcomes, while image-serving exceptions return a server error. There is no alternate image store or remote-service fallback.

Evidence: HomeController.java:37–97, DetailController.java:38–58, PhotoServiceImpl.java:112–185, PhotoFileController.java:44–86, upload.js:176–185.

Business Workflow Sequence

The primary upload flow below shows normal per-file outcomes; transaction-completion failures and unexpected controller lookup failures can escape that response handling. There is no circuit breaker; alternatives show actual rejection and error behavior.

Business Rules & Decision Logic

Validation and acceptance

  • Client upload screening: accept JPEG, PNG, GIF, or WebP MIME types and files no larger than 10 MiB. Empty selections do nothing; the client does not reject zero-length files here. Client checks are advisory. upload.js:60–87
  • Nonempty batch: a null/empty file list returns a bad-request result. Otherwise the response is normally successful at the HTTP level even if every file is rejected; its business success flag is true only when at least one display summary was collected. HomeController.java:62–97
  • Server upload acceptance: lowercase the submitted MIME type and compare it with the configured allowlist; require a positive file length not exceeding the configured byte limit. Default configuration matches the client types and 10 MiB limit. A missing MIME type reaches the generic upload-error catch rather than a dedicated validation message. PhotoServiceImpl.java:86–110, PhotoServiceImpl.java:186–190, application.properties:28–30
  • Image-dimension safety: when a header reader is available, reject images exceeding 40,000,000 pixels. An I/O exception rejects the upload; other dimension-extraction exceptions permit continuation without dimensions. If no reader recognizes the content, dimensions remain absent and upload can continue: the MIME allowlist is not a guarantee of decodable image content. PhotoServiceImpl.java:34–35, PhotoServiceImpl.java:117–158
  • Declared entity constraints: original/stored filenames must be nonblank and at most 255 characters; compatibility path is at most 500 characters; file size must be present and positive; MIME type must be nonblank and at most 50 characters; upload time must be present. These are entity annotations, not an explicit controller validation pass. Image content is nullable in the entity, but delivery treats absent content as not found. Photo.java:28–91, PhotoFileController.java:57–62
  • Request limits versus batch policy: multipart configuration limits each file to 10 MB and each request to 50 MB before business processing. A ten-files-per-upload property is declared but is not consumed by the traced controller/service/browser flow; it must not be presented as enforced behavior. application.properties:24–30, HomeController.java:57–91, PhotoServiceImpl.java:37–47, upload.js:60–100

Lifecycle, decisions, and computed presentation

  • Lifecycle: submitted file → rejected outcome or saved Photo → optional permanent deletion. There is no explicit status machine, approval state, deduplication check, or user-to-photo ownership relationship. Photo identity and upload time are generated on construction; the compatibility filename is separately randomized. Photo.java:93–107, PhotoServiceImpl.java:112–115, PhotoServiceImpl.java:160–177, PhotoServiceImpl.java:198–217
  • Chronological navigation: gallery ordering is descending upload time. Previous selects the first older result ordered newest first; next selects the first newer result ordered oldest first. Comparisons are strict, so equal upload timestamps do not become neighbors through these queries; no tie-breaker is specified. PhotoRepository.java:22–56, PhotoServiceImpl.java:223–237
  • Computed display: browser cards format the upload timestamp, round bytes to displayed kilobytes, and include dimensions only when both values are present. New cards are prepended; a complete gallery reload obtains authoritative timestamp ordering. upload.js:154–198, HomeController.java:37–41

Cross-cutting business behavior

  • Transactions: PhotoServiceImpl has class-level transactional behavior; reads and navigation explicitly use read-only transactions. Each externally invoked upload/delete service operation has its own boundary, not one transaction spanning the controller's batch loop. Save exceptions caught inside the service become failed outcomes where possible, but transaction commit/rollback exceptions may surface at the proxy boundary after the method returns. No distributed transaction or saga is present. PhotoServiceImpl.java:28–30, PhotoServiceImpl.java:53–75, PhotoServiceImpl.java:172–190, HomeController.java:68–91
  • Errors and recovery: validation/read/save failures normally become per-file messages; retrieval/deletion failures are wrapped as runtime exceptions. Controllers provide the workflow-specific empty-gallery, redirect, flash-message, or file-response outcomes described above. No automatic retry, dead-letter queue, or compensation is implemented. PhotoServiceImpl.java:55–75, PhotoServiceImpl.java:150–190, PhotoServiceImpl.java:214–217
  • Audit/logging: upload rejection/success, deletion, retrieval failures, and content serving are logged with filenames and/or identifiers. Content serving also logs a short byte prefix. These are operational logs; no durable business audit entity or change-history workflow is defined. PhotoServiceImpl.java:86–102, PhotoServiceImpl.java:179–189, PhotoServiceImpl.java:203–216, PhotoFileController.java:45–72
  • Authenticated writes: upload and deletion require authentication; gallery, detail, and content reads are public. The configured account is assigned an administrator role, but the write rules check authentication rather than a specific role or photo ownership. Authentication is stateless HTTP Basic, and CSRF protection is disabled. Credentials and credential values are intentionally omitted. SecurityConfig.java:33–60

Version & Compatibility Risks

Spring Boot 2.7.18 is a legacy line outside community support; upgrading to Spring Boot 3 requires Java 17 or newer and migration from Java EE javax APIs to Jakarta APIs. The manifest currently targets Java 8 (pom.xml:8–11,23–26). Commons IO is explicitly pinned to the older 2.11.0 release (pom.xml:68–73) and warrants a current compatibility and advisory review. Exact Oracle JDBC and H2 versions cannot be verified from this manifest alone; no vulnerability scan or resolved compatibility assessment was performed.

Notable Observations

  • Most version selection is centralized in the Spring Boot parent; the explicit Commons IO pin is outside that alignment (pom.xml:8–13,30–101).
  • The JSON starter is categorized as a utility: its nearby “Image processing” comment does not itself declare a dedicated image-processing library (pom.xml:75–79).
  • DevTools is optional but has no explicit runtime scope or profile restriction. Optional controls downstream propagation; it does not by itself establish production packaging behavior (pom.xml:95–100).
  • No direct messaging, caching, logging or observability dependencies are declared. Starter transitives may supply additional libraries, but no lockfile or local BOM content establishes their exact graph (pom.xml:30–101).

Data Architecture & Persistence Layer

The persistence layer has one JPA entity, Photo, containing both image metadata and binary content in one relational table. Spring Data JPA/Hibernate accesses Oracle in the default and Docker configurations; tests use an isolated in-memory H2 database. Sources: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/Photo.java:15-91, pom.xml:43-54,88-93, and the configuration files cited below.

Entity Model

erDiagram %% Photo Album owns photos; no mapped entity relationships. Photo { String id PK "photos.id; UUID string; length 36" String originalFileName "original_file_name; required; length 255" bytes photoData "photo_data; nullable LOB" String storedFileName "stored_file_name; required; length 255" String filePath "file_path; nullable; length 500" Long fileSize "file_size; required; Oracle NUMBER 19 digits" String mimeType "mime_type; required; length 50" LocalDateTime uploadedAt "uploaded_at; required; indexed" Integer width "width; nullable" Integer height "height; nullable" }

Photo maps to photos, with a nonunique index on uploaded_at. Its constructor assigns a UUID string and local upload timestamp; the timestamp column also declares an Oracle database-time default. The binary field uses @Lob without a lazy-fetch override. There are no foreign keys, relationship annotations, association cascades, or bidirectional links; no relationship edges are therefore invented in the diagram. Sources: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/Photo.java:15-97.

storedFileName and filePath are compatibility metadata, not an external blob-store reference used by the current persistence implementation. Image content is saved with the entity and served from its byte array (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:112-124,160-174; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/PhotoFileController.java:53-69). UploadResult is a nonpersistent result object, not another entity (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/UploadResult.java:3-10).

Transactions are declared at service-class level. Listing, ID lookup, and previous/next reads override this with read-only transactions; upload and deletion retain the class-level transaction semantics (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:28-30,53-71,81-82,172-185,198-210,223-236).

Key Repository Methods

All methods belong to PhotoRepository extends JpaRepository in src/main/java/com/photoalbum/repository/PhotoRepository.java:15-100. Standard inherited CRUD methods are omitted below; custom queries are all native SQL.

ServiceRepositoryNotable MethodsPurpose
Photo AlbumPhotoRepositoryList findAllOrderByUploadedAtDesc()Returns all photo rows newest-first, including the BLOB column. Source: lines 18-27.
Photo AlbumPhotoRepositoryList findPhotosUploadedBefore(LocalDateTime uploadedAt)Returns up to ten rows strictly older than the timestamp, descending, using Oracle ROWNUM. Source: lines 29-42.
Photo AlbumPhotoRepositoryList findPhotosUploadedAfter(LocalDateTime uploadedAt)Returns newer rows in ascending order, without a SQL row limit; substitutes a default for null compatibility paths using Oracle NVL. Source: lines 44-56.
Photo AlbumPhotoRepositoryList findPhotosByUploadMonth(String year, String month)Filters timestamps using Oracle TO_CHAR, then orders newest-first. Source: lines 58-71.
Photo AlbumPhotoRepositoryList findPhotosWithPagination(int startRow, int endRow)Selects an inclusive, one-based row range with nested Oracle ROWNUM queries. Source: lines 73-87.
Photo AlbumPhotoRepositoryList findPhotosWithStatistics()Returns photo columns plus file-size rank and running size totals via SQL analytical functions. Source: lines 89-100.

These queries couple persistence to Oracle syntax; configuring H2 alone does not establish equivalent behavior for them. The service uses ordered listing and timestamp navigation queries, taking the first navigation result; no cross-service bulk aggregation interface or stored-procedure invocation was found (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:53-57,223-237).

Data Ownership Boundaries

One application persistence boundary owns the photos table. Metadata and image BLOBs are colocated in its Oracle schema rather than split across a database and an object-storage service. The test profile replaces that store with an in-memory H2 database; it is not a second production datastore (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/Photo.java:15-91; src/main/resources/application.properties:9-21; src/test/resources/application-test.properties:1-10).

PhotoServiceImpl directly accesses its injected repository for both reads and writes. No separate read model, event-sourced store, outbox, other service's tables, inter-service data calls, or gateway aggregation methods were identified in this persistence layer. Read-only transaction annotations separate transaction intent, not CQRS storage ownership (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:37-45,53-75,172-174,198-210,223-237).
